lessons.title: Deep Work Is Rare and Valuable
lessons.key_idea: The ability to focus intensely is becoming more valuable just as it becomes rarer, which makes it a professional superpower.

lessons.title: Why Busyness Feels Like Productivity
lessons.key_idea: Without clear ways to measure output, workplaces default to visible busyness like fast email replies, which crowds out deep work.

lessons.title: Choose Your Depth Philosophy
lessons.key_idea: Deep work sticks when you pick a scheduling style that fits your life and support it with rituals for where, when, and how you work.

lessons.title: Train Your Brain to Embrace Boredom
lessons.key_idea: Concentration is a skill you weaken every time you reach for distraction, so you must practice resisting it, even in idle moments.

lessons.title: Use Tools Like a Craftsman
lessons.key_idea: Adopt a tool like social media only if its benefits to your most important goals clearly outweigh its costs, not just because it offers some benefit.

lessons.title: Drain the Shallows
lessons.key_idea: Plan your day in blocks, set a fixed end time, and make yourself harder to reach so that shallow tasks shrink to fit.

lessons.title: A Deep Life Is a Good Life
lessons.key_idea: Deep work does more than boost output; by directing your attention toward meaningful challenges, it shapes a more satisfying life.

plan.title: Deep Work
plan.author: Cal Newport
plan.confidence_note: I know this book's structure, core hypothesis, and four rules in detail, including most of its key examples and practical strategies.
plan.one_liner: Focus is becoming rare just as it becomes priceless. Here is how to reclaim it.
plan.summary: Cal Newport, a computer science professor, argues that the ability to concentrate without distraction on demanding tasks is becoming rarer just as it becomes more valuable. He calls this deep work, and contrasts it with shallow work: emails, meetings, and logistics that anyone could do while distracted. In the first half, he makes the case that deep work helps you learn hard things quickly and produce excellent results. He shows how modern workplaces quietly undermine it by treating busyness as a sign of productivity. He also argues that a focused life is a more meaningful one. In the second half, he offers four rules: build routines that protect deep work, train yourself to tolerate boredom, be choosy about social media and other tools, and ruthlessly limit shallow tasks.
